title: Global Traffic Distribution for E-commerce Resilience
business: A global retail firm operating a web-based storefront across multiple continents needs to ensure high availability for its customers.
problem: The firm faces regional outages and traffic spikes that cause downtime when users are routed to a single, overloaded data center.
solution: Google Cloud Load Balancing provides managed global traffic distribution, allowing the firm to route users to the nearest healthy backend instance regardless of their geographic location.
steps: Define a Global Forwarding Rule to direct incoming traffic to a specific target proxy.
Configure a URL Map to route requests based on hostnames and path rules to backend services.
Create Backend Services that group regional instance groups or serverless endpoints.
Set up Health Checks to monitor the status of backend instances and remove unhealthy ones from the rotation.
outcome: Improved service reliability and reduced latency by ensuring traffic is always served by the closest available healthy infrastructure.
limitation: Global load balancers require careful configuration of health checks; if health checks are too aggressive, they may cause flapping where healthy instances are incorrectly marked as down. Check this by monitoring the 'Health Check Status' metrics in the monitoring console.

questions.question: In Global Traffic Distribution for E-commerce Resilience, what is the primary purpose of using Google Cloud Load Balancing?
options: To provide managed global traffic distribution and ensure high availability.
To replace the need for regional instance groups entirely.
To automatically lower the cost of compute resources.
To act as a primary database for retail transactions.
questions.explanation: The scenario identifies that the firm needs to route users to the nearest healthy backend to avoid regional outages, which is the core function of the load balancer.
questions.evidence: Google Cloud Load Balancing provides managed global traffic distribution, allowing the firm to route users to the nearest healthy backend instance regardless of their geographic location.

questions.question: In Global Traffic Distribution for E-commerce Resilience, what is a potential limitation of the implementation?
options: The load balancer cannot handle traffic from multiple continents.
Aggressive health checks may cause healthy instances to be marked as down.
URL maps are not supported for global traffic routing.
Backend services must be located in the same region as the user.
questions.explanation: The limitation section explicitly warns that overly aggressive health checks can lead to incorrect status reporting, known as flapping.
questions.evidence: if health checks are too aggressive, they may cause flapping where healthy instances are incorrectly marked as down.
